query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys develop and retain a protective oxide layer because key oxide‐forming elements (such as Al and Cr) selectively segregate to the surface under high-temperature conditions, where they form continuous, adherent oxides that slow down further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: HEAs with a baseline equiatomic composition lacking protective element enrichment.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by enriching it with protective elements (e.g., increased Al and/or Cr content) and perform high-temperature oxidation testing.
generation.conditions: Oxidation tests conducted at 800–1200°C in an ambient pressure oxygen atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale (e.g., Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3) that acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the protective elements segregate to the surface and preferentially oxidize, forming a robust and uniform oxide layer. This scale minimizes further oxygen diffusion into the alloy and thus improves the oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys enriched with protective elements will show slower oxidation kinetics, thinner and more uniform oxide layers, and better preservation of the underlying metal structure compared to baseline alloys.
generation.baseline: HEA compositions with no enrichment in protective oxide-forming elements.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under high-temperature, oxygen-rich conditions (800–1200°C, ambient pressure) and may not hold in reducing atmospheres or under rapid thermal cycling conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of different enrichment levels on oxidation kinetics and the possible interaction with other alloying elements remain uncertain; long-term stability beyond tested durations also requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HEA samples: one with a baseline equiatomic composition and one with increased content of protective elements (e.g., Al and/or Cr enrichment). Subject both groups to identical high-temperature oxidation tests at 800–1200°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere. Use in-situ surface characterization techniques (such as XPS and SEM/EDS) at multiple oxidation time intervals to monitor oxide formation, layer continuity, and elemental distribution.
measurements: Elemental distribution at the oxide/metal interface
Adherence and structural integrity of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enriched samples do not consistently exhibit statistically significant improvements in oxidation resistance (e.g., reduced oxidation rate, thinner and more continuous oxide layers) compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis that selective protective-element segregation governs the development and retention of a protective oxide layer is falsified.

In this study, the high-temperature oxidation behavior of a series of AlTiNiCuCox high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was explored. The AlTiNiCuCox (x = 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5) series HEAs were prepared using a vacuum induction melting furnace, in which three kinds of AlTiNiCuCox (x = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5) alloys with different Co contents were oxidized at 800 °C for 100 h, and their oxidation kinetic curves were determined. The microstructure, morphology, structure, and phase composition of the oxide film surface and cross-sectional layers of AlTiNiCuCox series HEAs were analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive spectrometry (EDS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). The influence of Co content on the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the HEAs was discussed, and the oxidation mechanism was summarized. The results indicate that, at 800 °C, the AlTiNiCuCox (x = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5) series HEAs had dense oxide films and certain high-temperature oxidation resistance. With increasing Co content, the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the alloys also increased. cited_evidence.text: Figure 8 presents line scanning energy spectrum diagrams of the cross section of the AlTiNiCuCo1.0 alloy oxide layer after oxidation for 50 and 100 h at 800 °C. After 100 h oxidation, the oxide film was thicker than that after 50 h, but the change in thickness was not apparent. This indicates that the oxide film of an HEA of this composition under high-temperature oxidation is relatively dense and plays a certain protective role for the alloy; thus, the alloy has better high-temperature oxidation resistance. It can be seen from Figure 8a, representing 50 h oxidation, that the oxide layer still contained large amounts of Al, Ti, and O elements. It was presumed that there were mainly two oxides, Al2O3 and TiO2, in the oxide layer. After oxidation for 100 h, the contents of Al and Ti in the oxide layer were greater, and the content of Co was significantly increased. Combining this with XRD analysis results, it was found that there were three oxides present: CoAl2O4, Al2O3, and TiO2.

occupying_moves.technique: systematic high-temperature oxidation tests combined with in-situ surface characterization (e.g., XPS, SEM/EDS)
occupying_moves.conditions: HEA samples with controlled variations in the concentration of key elements (e.g., Cr or Al) are tested at 800–1200°C in oxidizing atmospheres (ambient pressure), with measurements comparing oxide development kinetics against baseline compositions lacking the protective element enrichment.

chosen.technique: systematic high-temperature oxidation tests combined with in-situ XPS and SEM/EDS analysis
chosen.conditions: HEA samples with controlled differences in the concentration of the key protective elements (e.g., Cr and/or Al) assessed under oxidizing conditions at 800–1200°C and ambient pressure to reveal changes in oxide layer formation and retention versus baseline alloys.
chosen.why: This move directly fills the niche by testing the mechanistic hypothesis that the oxidation resistance in high-entropy alloys is governed by a controlled selective oxidation process which enriches critical oxide-forming elements at the surface. A controlled variable experiment contrasting alloys with and without enriched protective elements using standard high-temperature oxidation tests and in-situ surface analyses provides a clear, measurable pathway to validate or falsify the hypothesis.
